question: Can a factorized, self-consistent mean-field posterior explain the onset and generalization of feature learning in finite two-layer ReLU networks, and does adding coordinate-wise automatic relevance determination recover the input-feature selection that ordinary mean field misses?

key_findings.claim: The paper constructs a static mean-field approximation to the Bayesian/SGLD posterior of a two-layer ReLU network, with each neuron sampled from a self-consistent one-particle Gibbs distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Starting from the squared-loss Gibbs posterior, the authors replace pairwise neuron interactions by expectations under an exchangeable one-particle law. The resulting effective energy contains a data-alignment term J_Y and a self-consistent interaction field J_S plus the Gaussian weight prior; iterating an inner sampler and outer field update supplies the numerical mean-field solution.

anchors.section: 3 A Simple Mean Field Model / Equations 5-7

key_findings.claim: At the neural-network Gaussian-process scaling, the interaction vanishes and the predictor reduces to kernel ridge regression, while the finite-interaction scaling is intended to model learned features.
key_findings.evidence: The paper identifies gamma=1/2 as the NNGP limit and derives a ReLU-kernel ridge predictor with ridge proportional to kappa squared divided by the output-weight prior variance. At the mean-field scaling used in the experiments, the J_S field couples the one-particle law back to its own feature covariance, so the effective kernel changes with the data.

anchors.section: D.1 Recovering the NNGP Limit / Equations 55-59

key_findings.claim: Plain mean field predicts a sharp increase in specialization and improves over the NNGP baseline, but substantially underestimates the post-onset generalization of the trained network.
key_findings.evidence: On sparse parity, both SGLD and the ordinary mean-field simulation develop a nonzero specialization order parameter as sample size increases, whereas NNGP changes smoothly. The ordinary mean-field test-MSE curve remains visibly above SGLD after the transition; this empirical miss motivates the ARD extension rather than validating plain mean field as quantitatively accurate.

anchors.section: 3.2 Feature Learning as a Phase Transition / Equation 11

key_findings.claim: The exact scalar fixed-point equation displayed in the main text does not support the claimed exactly-zero order parameter below a critical point when the data-alignment field is nonzero.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 writes the right-hand side as a positive multiple of (1-m_S) times an expectation of J_S(w)^2 divided by a positive denominator. Evaluated at m_S=0, this is generally positive for a finite teacher signal. The authors themselves call J_Y an external field, which explicitly breaks the symmetry. The exact integral can therefore yield a small crossover, but not the stated m_S=0 branch without an additional approximation or boundary argument.

anchors.section: D.2 Fixed Point Equation for the Order Parameter

key_findings.claim: The appendix's critical-threshold formula is obtained only after a sharply peaked, optimal-direction approximation, not as an exact consequence of the original mean-field integral.
key_findings.evidence: The proof first assumes concentration around a MAP-like weight direction and replaces the integral equation by an optimization over a scale alpha. The nonzero solution is then read from an expression for alpha squared and the infeasible negative region is effectively placed at the boundary. The main-text presentation does not keep these additional assumptions visible, and the appendix's criterion checks when the reduced right-hand side ceases to vanish rather than a derivative-crossing stability condition for the exact fixed point.

key_findings.claim: The proposed explanation for the quantitative gap is input-feature selection: finite neurons reinforce a small subset of teacher coordinates, producing anisotropic and heavy-tailed first-layer weights that a single isotropic factorized law suppresses.
key_findings.evidence: SGLD simulations show a subset of neurons with large support-aligned components and increasingly heavy-tailed marginal weight histograms after the onset. The paper argues that neuron-neuron dependencies select coordinates collectively, while ordinary mean field averages across permutation-equivalent features and retains a lighter-tailed isotropic prior.

anchors.section: 3.3 What Mean Field Misses: Input Feature Selection
A.3 Weight histograms and sparsity diagnostics

key_findings.claim: Mean-field ARD introduces coordinate-specific Gaussian precisions with Gamma hyperpriors and empirical-Bayes updates, creating a feedback loop that amplifies coordinates with large posterior second moments.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 13-16 replace the isotropic first-layer prior by per-coordinate precisions rho_j. The posterior-rate update depends on the average squared j-th weight, so a coordinate with more posterior mass receives lower precision and hence larger future variance. The intended outer loop alternates sampling weights under the current precisions and updating these precisions.

anchors.section: 4 Mean Field with Automatic Relevance Determination / Equations 13-16

key_findings.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves amplification conditional on an already-existing dimension-independent support gap; it does not prove that ARD or SGLD spontaneously discovers the relevant coordinates.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem assumes that at an O(1) outer iteration t_0, every relevant coordinate's posterior second moment exceeds every irrelevant coordinate's by a constant epsilon_0 independent of ambient dimension. That assumption is the essential feature-selection seed. Under it, the appendix derives a support-favored precision separation and a critical-noise scaling, but it does not establish that the required gap emerges from symmetric initialization or finite-sample dynamics.

key_findings.claim: The advertised dimensional improvement relies on additional asymptotics and contains an internal width-versus-sample notation error.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem states a critical noise-squared scale improving from order 1/sqrt(dk) for plain mean field to 1/sqrt(k) for MF-ARD. The proof invokes a large-curvature asymptotic even though the experiments use fixed small k=2 or 4, where its accuracy is not quantified. Theorem D.13 also calls N the number of training samples, whereas N denotes hidden width and P denotes sample count throughout the model and preceding derivations.

key_findings.claim: The printed MF-ARD algorithm cannot implement the coordinate-wise mechanism used by the theory and figures because its Gamma-rate update is scalar.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 145 and Algorithm 1 update beta_post using the sum of full vector norms over particles, then assign rho=alpha_post/beta_post. This produces one shared scalar precision. Equations 15-16 require a separate beta_j proportional to the sum of w_bj squared for each coordinate. As printed, the algorithm collapses ARD back to isotropic shrinkage and therefore cannot generate coordinate selection; an unreported implementation change is necessary to reproduce the MF-ARD results.

key_findings.claim: The gradients in the numerical appendix are inconsistent with the stated squared-error objective and appear to double-count a neuron's self-contribution.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix defines residual r=y-f and loss P^{-1}||r||^2. Direct differentiation gives a data gradient proportional to -2 r times the neuron's feature. Equations 140 and 143 instead use r-s a phi inside the update and then add a separate self-covariance term, even though r already includes that neuron's contribution. A leave-one-out residual would require the opposite sign. Thus the displayed SGLD/mean-field update is not the gradient of Equation 141.

key_findings.claim: MF-ARD visually tracks SGLD better than plain mean field on two sparse synthetic teachers, but the match is not quantified and is evaluated on the same narrow settings used to develop the mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: For d=35, k=4 parity and d=18, k=2 fourth-order Hermite single-index targets, MF-ARD's test-MSE curves and two-dimensional weight-density heatmaps are closer to SGLD than ordinary mean field. The paper provides no curve-fit error, likelihood, held-out task, calibration interval, or preregistered parameter prediction. The single-index figure omits plain mean field and NNGP, and the parity heatmaps are qualitative.

key_findings.claim: The claimed prior calibration is mathematically false for the inverse precision and especially problematic for the single-index hyperparameter.
key_findings.evidence: The paper sets beta_0=alpha_0/d so E[rho]=d and says this matches the isotropic variance 1/d in expectation. For rho distributed as Gamma(alpha,beta) under the paper's rate convention, E[1/rho]=beta/(alpha-1), not 1/E[rho]. With alpha_0=4 it equals 4/(3d), and with the reported single-index alpha_0=0.1 the inverse-precision mean diverges. The experiments also initialize rho deterministically at d and update it by empirical Bayes, which is distinct from sampling or integrating the heavy-tailed hierarchical prior invoked in the explanation.

key_findings.claim: Two independent appendix inconsistencies weaken the claimed limiting derivation: the exponent statement for gamma and the kernel-ridge factor of two.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.1 says N^(1-gamma) tends to zero for gamma>1/2, which is false for 1/2<gamma<1. Later, Equation 58 yields the same ridge kappa squared over sigma_a squared as main-text Equation 10, but the prose after Equation 59 defines the ridge with an extra factor two. These do not by themselves overturn the empirical plots, but they prevent the written asymptotic argument from being treated as an internally exact derivation.

key_findings.claim: The SGLD experiments do not establish equilibrium-posterior sampling, so agreement with a static Bayesian mean-field model may partly reflect finite-time optimizer behavior.
key_findings.evidence: The posterior interpretation is exact only for an infinitesimal-step stationary Langevin process. The experiments use finite, scheduled learning rates and report terminal trajectories after up to millions of steps, with no burn-in, mixing, autocorrelation, effective-sample-size, detailed-balance, or multiple-chain diagnostic. Consequently, SGLD is an empirical stochastic-training reference, not demonstrated posterior ground truth.

method.core_idea: Approximate the finite two-layer network's Gibbs posterior by a self-consistent single-neuron distribution, diagnose the resulting feature-learning transition, and augment the prior with learned coordinate-wise precisions so the factorized theory can represent sparse input-feature selection.
method.mechanism: A two-layer ReLU network is trained with SGLD under Gaussian priors. Ordinary mean field replaces cross-neuron sums by expectations under a shared particle distribution and alternates an inner Langevin sampler with updates of the induced self-interaction field. MF-ARD additionally alternates per-coordinate Gamma/Gaussian empirical-Bayes precision updates, ideally lowering precision on coordinates whose sampled weights have elevated second moments. Order parameters, posterior weight densities, kernel-ridge limits, and synthetic test errors are then compared with direct finite-network SGLD.
assumptions: Neurons are exchangeable and their posterior dependencies can be replaced by a product one-particle law plus a self-consistent field.
The finite-step SGLD runs are sufficiently close to samples from the intended Gibbs posterior despite absent mixing diagnostics.
Sparse parity and sparse single-index teachers capture the feature-selection mechanism relevant to broader representation learning.
For the phase-boundary proof, the posterior is sharply concentrated around a single optimal direction and an amplitude optimization represents the full integral fixed point.
The optimal ReLU direction for sparse parity has equal relevant-coordinate weights and exactly zero irrelevant-coordinate weights.
The support-aligned posterior second-moment gap assumed at iteration t_0 appears from symmetric initialization before ARD amplification begins.
The curvature parameter is large enough for the asymptotic used to simplify the MF and MF-ARD critical-noise expressions, including at k=2 or 4.
Coordinate-wise empirical-Bayes precision updates adequately stand in for the integrated hierarchical Bayesian prior used to motivate heavy tails.
Particle counts of 512 or 1024 and finite inner chains accurately approximate the self-consistent expectations.
The numerical update actually used in the experiments differs appropriately from the scalar ARD and inconsistent gradients printed in Algorithm 1.
Visual curve and density agreement is sufficient evidence of quantitative explanation without a formal goodness-of-fit statistic.
The selected noise, temperature, prior, clipping, moving-average, and inner/outer-step hyperparameters do not create the observed transition artifactually.

techniques.role: Frames stochastic training of the finite network as approximate posterior sampling under squared loss and Gaussian priors.
Replaces pairwise neuron coupling by an effective one-particle field determined by expectations under the same law.
Recovers a fixed ReLU-kernel ridge predictor when the interaction term disappears.
Measures alignment of posterior features with the sparse teacher subspace and operationally locates the onset.
Reduces the fixed-point integral to an optimal direction and amplitude to derive a closed-form threshold.
Assigns a learned precision to every input coordinate to permit anisotropic posterior variance.
Turns sampled per-coordinate second moments into updated precisions with a heavy-tailed hierarchical-prior interpretation.
Numerically solves the ordinary and ARD self-consistency equations using particles, inner Langevin steps, and moving-average field updates.
Tests a high-order sparse target whose relevant coordinates are permutation symmetric and hard for a fixed kernel.
Provides a second sparse nonlinear target with a low-dimensional teacher direction.

evaluations.setting: Sparse parity with ambient dimension d=35, support k=4, width N=512, and P varied across the transition.
evaluations.metric: Held-out mean-squared error over three independent networks/configuration.
evaluations.result: SGLD drops sharply after the onset; MF-ARD follows the post-onset curve much more closely than ordinary mean field, while NNGP remains substantially worse. Exact numeric curve values and fit error are not tabulated.
evaluations.baseline: Finite-network SGLD, ordinary mean field, and NNGP/kernel ridge regression.

evaluations.setting: The same sparse-parity sweep over training-set size.
evaluations.result: SGLD and MF-ARD show a sharp rise near P around five thousand; ordinary mean field rises more gradually and to a lower level, while NNGP has no comparable learned-feature transition.
evaluations.baseline: SGLD versus ordinary MF, MF-ARD, and NNGP.

evaluations.setting: Sparse-parity first-layer posterior at selected pre- and post-transition sample sizes.
evaluations.metric: Marginal weight histograms and qualitative support-coordinate heavy-tail/sparsity patterns.
evaluations.result: SGLD develops heavier support-coordinate tails and a selected subset of large aligned weights; MF-ARD reproduces more of this anisotropy than ordinary mean field. No tail index, distance, likelihood, or uncertainty is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary isotropic MF and the finite SGLD network.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional slices of learned weight distributions for the parity task.
evaluations.result: MF-ARD heatmaps appear closer to SGLD than plain MF after the transition, but modes and density mass are not compared quantitatively.
evaluations.baseline: SGLD and ordinary MF posterior-density visualizations.

evaluations.setting: Fourth-order Hermite single-index target with d=18, teacher support k=2, N=1024, and P varied; four runs/configuration.
evaluations.result: MF-ARD follows the SGLD error transition qualitatively. The displayed comparison omits ordinary MF and NNGP, so incremental benefit on this second task is not established.
evaluations.baseline: Finite-network SGLD only in the main single-index plot.

evaluations.setting: Analytical sparse-parity teacher under the peaked optimal-direction approximation.
evaluations.metric: Critical noise-squared scaling in ambient dimension d and support size k.
evaluations.result: The reduced derivation reports order 1/sqrt(dk) for ordinary MF and order 1/sqrt(k) for MF-ARD, conditional on an O(1) support-moment gap and a large-curvature approximation.
evaluations.baseline: Plain MF threshold versus ARD-augmented MF threshold.

evaluations.setting: Noise-level sweeps around the parity onset.
evaluations.result: MF-ARD captures the qualitative shift of the onset and the existence of a beneficial-noise regime, but the plotted boundary visibly differs from SGLD and has no confidence interval or numerical discrepancy measure.
evaluations.baseline: SGLD, plain MF, and NNGP across noise.

evaluations.setting: Long-run numerical solution with 512/1024 particles, 2-12 inner SGLD steps, moving-average fields, and up to roughly 7.5 million outer epochs/steps depending on the task.
evaluations.metric: Convergence judged from terminal prediction and order-parameter curves.
evaluations.result: The reported curves stabilize enough to compare visually, but no convergence tolerance, chain diagnostic, integration error, seed list, or wall-clock/compute comparison is supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Direct network SGLD under separately tuned finite-step schedules.

limitations: Author-stated: the analysis is restricted to two-layer networks and does not cover deeper, convolutional, recurrent, or attention architectures.
Author-stated: the proposed input-feature-selection picture targets sparse teachers and may not describe distributed or smooth representations.
Author-stated: the equilibrium posterior theory does not describe transient training dynamics.

Reviewer-identified: the exact fixed-point equation has a nonzero external field and does not yield the claimed exactly-zero subcritical order parameter; the sharp threshold comes from a later MAP/boundary approximation.

Reviewer-identified: the proof that the optimal parity ReLU neuron has equal support weights and no off-support component is informal; ReLU nonlinearity prevents orthogonal noise from simply averaging out of J_S.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 4.1 assumes the dimension-independent support gap that constitutes the essential feature-selection event, so it proves amplification rather than discovery.
Reviewer-identified: the large-curvature approximation underlying the dimension scaling is not error-controlled for the small support sizes used in experiments.
Reviewer-identified: the printed Algorithm 1 uses one scalar Gamma-rate update and therefore cannot implement coordinate-wise ARD.
Reviewer-identified: the displayed inner-loop gradients do not match the stated squared-error loss, leaving the exact implementation and reproducibility unresolved.
Reviewer-identified: the Gamma prior is not variance-matched as claimed; for alpha_0=0.1 the prior inverse-precision expectation is infinite.
Reviewer-identified: only two synthetic sparse tasks are tested, with no real data, non-sparse negative control, SGD/Adam training, depth, convolution, or attention experiment.

Reviewer-identified: comparisons use visual curves and heatmaps without fit statistics, posterior predictive calibration, raw tables, held-out configurations, or uncertainty for the theory-to-SGLD discrepancy.
Reviewer-identified: the single-index experiment excludes ordinary MF and NNGP, weakening the cross-task ablation of ARD's incremental effect.
Reviewer-identified: alpha_0 changes from 4 on parity to 0.1 on the single-index task despite a claim of insensitivity, and no sensitivity sweep is shown.
Reviewer-identified: three or four repetitions are used without clear error-bar definitions on every plot, seeds, evaluation-set size, or statistical tests.
Reviewer-identified: no posterior-mixing, burn-in, autocorrelation, or effective-sample-size evidence supports treating finite-step SGLD as equilibrium ground truth.
Reviewer-identified: the particle mean-field solver is itself computationally intensive and is not benchmarked as a cheaper predictive method than simulating the original finite network.
Reviewer-identified: no code URL, exact random seeds, raw arrays, numerical-integration accuracy, or implementation correction for the appendix equations is provided.
failure_modes: With any finite teacher-alignment field, the exact order parameter can exhibit a smooth crossover rather than a genuine symmetry-breaking transition, making a threshold depend on arbitrary numerical resolution.
A factorized one-particle law can average over several permutation-equivalent selected-feature states and erase the cross-neuron correlations responsible for finite-network specialization.
If the assumed support-moment seed does not arise, ARD preserves the symmetric solution or amplifies random irrelevant-coordinate fluctuations instead of finding the teacher support.
Coordinate-wise empirical Bayes can lock onto sampling noise at small P, producing false sparsity and overconfident precisions.
Precision clipping, exponential moving averages, or too few inner Langevin steps can manufacture or shift the apparent phase boundary.
A heavy-tailed hierarchical prior can improve sparse targets while overfitting noise or harming tasks whose useful representation is dense and rotationally distributed.
The scalar update in the published algorithm collapses all coordinate precisions together, eliminating the intended ARD mechanism entirely.
The inconsistent residual gradient can double-count a particle's self-feature and converge to a different fixed point from the written posterior objective.
Finite-step SGLD can remain trapped in one selected-feature basin, so apparent posterior sparsity may be metastable optimization rather than equilibrium Bayesian mass.
The optimal-direction approximation can miss multimodal, broad, or multiple-feature posterior states and produce a spurious closed-form critical threshold.
Helpful noise may disappear under a different optimizer, schedule, batch size, width, or posterior temperature because those variables are not separated experimentally.
The claimed dimension-free ARD threshold can fail when k grows with d, the curvature is not large, the teacher weights are unequal, or irrelevant features correlate with the target.
A coordinate-aligned ARD prior cannot detect sparse structure expressed in an unknown rotated basis without first learning that basis.
Curve agreement can be obtained by task-specific alpha_0, clipping, or iteration choices without the inferred mechanism being causally correct.
reusable_insights: Distinguish an exact self-consistency equation from a MAP, concentration, or boundary approximation before calling its crossover a phase transition.
When a purported order parameter has a nonzero external field, test the fixed-point equation at zero explicitly; exact symmetry breaking generally requires the field to vanish.
A theorem that assumes an already-separated feature moment proves reinforcement, not feature discovery; state the seed mechanism as a separate claim.
Coordinate-wise ARD requires coordinate-wise sufficient statistics in both equations and code; a norm-summed scalar update is a decisive reproducibility check.
Verify symbolic optimizer updates by differentiating the stated loss, especially when residual definitions and self-interaction corrections coexist.
Matching E[rho] does not match E[1/rho]; hierarchical precision priors should be calibrated in the variance quantity actually used by the network.
Use dense or rotated-teacher negative controls to determine whether a sparsity prior explains learning broadly or merely encodes the evaluation task.
Quantify theory-to-simulation agreement with held-out parameter settings, curve-distance metrics, uncertainty, and preregistered predictions rather than heatmap resemblance alone.
Treat finite-step Langevin optimization as posterior sampling only after reporting mixing and stationarity diagnostics.
Separate interpretive tractability from computational efficiency: a particle fixed-point solver can be conceptually simpler while costing more than the original model.
For sparse-feature theories, compare coordinate selection with basis-invariant low-rank or subspace selection to expose dependence on privileged input axes.
Keep width and sample-count notation distinct throughout asymptotic statements because interchanging them changes the claimed scaling regime.
open_questions: Can the exact mean-field integral exhibit a mathematically sharp transition when J_Y is nonzero, or only a finite-size crossover whose operational threshold depends on tolerance?
Can one rigorously optimize the ReLU parity alignment ratio over both support and orthogonal components instead of assuming the equal-support direction?
From symmetric initialization, what finite-sample or dynamical mechanism creates the O(1), dimension-independent support second-moment gap required by Theorem 4.1?
Does a corrected coordinate-wise Algorithm 1 reproduce every reported MF-ARD curve, and what exact gradient/residual implementation generated the figures?
How accurate is the large-curvature threshold approximation at k=2 and k=4, and what are finite-k error bounds?
Does MF-ARD outperform plain MF on held-out sparse Boolean functions, unequal teacher weights, correlated covariates, and rotated sparse subspaces without retuning alpha_0?
What happens on dense single-index, smooth low-frequency, compositional, or deliberately non-sparse targets where input-axis selection should not help?
Can cluster, mixture, low-rank, or correlated mean-field families capture neuron co-selection directly without inserting coordinate sparsity through a hyperprior?
Do posterior chains mix between permutation-equivalent selected-feature states, and does the averaged equilibrium retain the same heavy tails as a single finite run?
Which measured statistic quantitatively predicts generalization beyond m_S: support recovery, tail index, learned-kernel spectrum, margin, or posterior predictive variance?
Can the theory extend to SGD/Adam, cross-entropy, minibatches, learned output weights, deeper networks, and normalization layers?
Is MF-ARD computationally competitive with direct finite-network simulation at matched error, and how do particle count and inner-chain length affect bias?
Would fully Bayesian integration over precisions, rather than empirical-Bayes point updates, preserve uncertainty and avoid early false-support lock-in?
How should the noise, prior, width, sample size, and task sparsity co-scale when k grows with d rather than remaining fixed?

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Directly studies a phase transition from a memorizing/kernel-like solution to a generalizing feature-learning solution in two-layer networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It focuses on grokking dynamics and a first-order transition, whereas the reviewed paper uses a static Bayesian mean-field posterior and adds coordinate-wise ARD. Its prior phase-transition account means the general phenomenon is not new; the ARD self-consistent explanation is the narrower differentiator.

competitive_landscape.title: From Kernels to Features: A Multi-Scale Adaptive Theory of Feature Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Provides a contemporary adaptive theory spanning kernel and feature-learning regimes.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its multi-scale adaptive kernel perspective targets training-time feature evolution rather than a factorized equilibrium Gibbs posterior. It is broader on the kernel-to-feature continuum, while the reviewed paper is more specific about sparse coordinate selection and ARD.

competitive_landscape.title: Critical Feature Learning in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Analyzes critical feature-learning behavior and transitions beyond fixed-kernel predictions.
competitive_landscape.difference: It addresses deep networks and critical scaling, while the reviewed work deliberately uses a simple two-layer Bayesian mean-field model. This weakens any broad priority claim for critical feature learning but not the specific MF-ARD construction.

competitive_landscape.title: Asymptotics of Feature Learning in Two-Layer Networks After One Gradient-Step
competitive_landscape.relationship: Gives a rigorous high-dimensional account of feature formation and generalization in two-layer networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies one gradient step in a controlled asymptotic regime rather than a long-run Gibbs equilibrium. It has stronger dynamical/asymptotic specificity, whereas the reviewed paper aims to match finite SGLD phase diagrams through a self-consistent posterior.

competitive_landscape.title: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective on the Spectrum of Learned Features and Asymptotic Generalization Capabilities
competitive_landscape.relationship: Connects learned feature spectra in two-layer networks to asymptotic generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It analyzes spectral structure through random-matrix limits rather than coordinate-wise posterior sparsity. It is an alternative mechanism and measurement framework that the reviewed paper does not compare against.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks Can Learn Representations with Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: Shows how two-layer networks can learn a small set of relevant representation directions and gain dimension-dependent sample efficiency over kernels.
competitive_landscape.difference: It supplies a gradient-descent representation-learning guarantee without Bayesian mean field or ARD. The reviewed theorem's sparse-direction benefit therefore sits in an established line; its proposed novelty is explaining finite SGLD with a minimal static mean-field correction.

competitive_landscape.title: The Merged-Staircase Property: A Necessary and Nearly Sufficient Condition for SGD Learning of Sparse Functions on Two-Layer Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Characterizes when SGD learns sparse Boolean functions with two-layer networks, directly overlapping the parity/sparse-function setting.
competitive_landscape.difference: It concerns algorithmic learnability and the structure of sparse functions, not a posterior mean-field approximation. It provides important negative task-structure context absent from the two favorable teachers in the reviewed paper.

competitive_landscape.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
competitive_landscape.relationship: Studies emergence of input-dependent features and their advantage over fixed-feature kernels.
competitive_landscape.difference: It analyzes gradient-based feature learning directly, whereas the reviewed paper uses equilibrium SGLD and mean-field self-consistency. It establishes that input-aligned feature emergence predates the paper's IFS terminology.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Kernel Predictors from Feature-Learning Infinite Limits of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Derives adaptive kernel predictors from infinite-width feature-learning limits and is a direct current alternative to a fixed NNGP baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: It makes the learned predictor adaptive through an infinite-limit kernel description rather than coordinate-wise empirical-Bayes precisions. The reviewed paper's distinction is its finite-neuron IFS diagnosis, but it does not benchmark this stronger adaptive-kernel baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamical Decoupling of Generalization and Overfitting in Large Two-Layer Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Provides a current dynamical account in which feature learning, generalization, and later overfitting can decouple in large two-layer networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its negative late-time feature-unlearning behavior challenges a purely static equilibrium interpretation. It postdates the reviewed arXiv submission and does not negate its historical claim, but it narrows the current usefulness of an equilibrium-only explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: Width-Robust Learnability in Mean-Field Bayesian Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later current work studies learnability and width robustness in Bayesian mean-field neural networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is a post-submission theoretical competitor focused on width-robust learnability rather than ARD reconstruction of SGLD feature-selection curves. Its existence limits present-day uniqueness of the broader Bayesian mean-field framing but not chronological novelty at submission.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a deliberately simple self-consistent mean-field model that predicts an onset of feature learning, identify input-feature selection as the correlation effect missed by ordinary mean field, and show that a minimal coordinate-wise ARD extension both matches finite-network SGLD quantitatively and removes the ambient-dimension penalty in the critical-noise scaling.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The distinctive empirical package is the side-by-side SGLD/MF/NNGP/MF-ARD phase diagram, order parameter, posterior-density visualization, and an ARD threshold calculation for sparse parity, plus a second sparse single-index illustration.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow combination of a static one-particle Gibbs mean field with learned coordinate precisions is plausibly distinctive, but the broad ingredients—feature-learning transitions, sparse relevant-direction benefits, adaptive kernels, ARD, and two-layer mean-field theory—are established. The strongest theorem assumes the support separation it is meant to explain, the exact fixed point does not have the claimed zero-field phase transition, and the printed algorithm cannot implement coordinate-wise ARD and uses gradients inconsistent with its loss. Accordingly, the work is best viewed as a suggestive interpretive model and empirical fit for two hand-chosen synthetic sparse tasks, not a validated general or reproducible quantitative theory of finite-network feature learning. Later 2025-2026 dynamical and Bayesian-mean-field competitors further narrow its current distinctiveness without changing submission-time chronology.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text audit of all 38/38 pages of the exact cached arXiv PDF, including references, Appendices A-E, every theorem/proof, Tables 1-2, Figures 1-7, equations, and Algorithm 1. Critical rendered-page checks confirmed the coordinate-wise-versus-scalar ARD contradiction on pages 35-36 and the residual-gradient inconsistency on page 35. The cached PDF header says it was published as an ICLR 2026 conference paper, while the official arXiv record checked on 2026-08-23 remains arXiv:2510.15174v1 submitted 2025-10-16; this reading is pinned to the exact PDF and hashes above, not an inferred later revision. Competitor records were checked against current official arXiv, OpenReview, or proceedings pages through 2026-08-23; post-submission work is explicitly labeled rather than used to retroactively negate historical novelty. No source page was missing from extracted text.
